title: Y-shaped arrays with all baseline lengths different
statement: A Y-shaped interferometer, like the Very Large Array, places its antennas on three straight arms that meet at 120 degrees. Put antennas at whole-number distances 1, 2, 3, ... from the centre (the centre itself unused). Two antennas on one arm at distances a and a' are |a - a'| apart; two on different arms are sqrt(a^2 + ab + b^2) apart. Each baseline length gives one sample of the visibility of a circularly symmetric source, so we ask that all N(N - 1)/2 baseline lengths be different. Let L(N) be the shortest arm length for which N antennas fit. We find L(N) exactly for N <= 12. The headline cell is N = 27, the number of antennas of the VLA: find a Y array of 27 antennas with all 351 baseline lengths different and arms shorter than 165 (ours).
submission: Text file: three lines, the distances (positive integers) of the antennas on each arm ('-' for an empty arm), 27 antennas in all.
score: the arm length, the largest distance used (smaller is better)

best_known.source: Quantavane (Arhan Canli), 9 November 2026: local search that moves one antenna at a time to the place creating the fewest repeated lengths, with a tabu list, shortening the arms while it succeeds (tools/src/yarray.c, mode ls)

context: Radio and optical interferometers sample the Fourier transform of the sky at the baselines between their telescopes, and many are Y-shaped: the VLA has 27 antennas on three arms at 120 degrees, CHARA six telescopes, MROI up to ten. Non-redundant designs avoid repeated baseline vectors, which on a Y is easy (baselines between different arms never repeat; each arm only needs a Golomb ruler). For a circularly symmetric source, such as a star's disc, the visibility depends only on the baseline length, and then repeated lengths waste samples: the question becomes one of distinct distances on three rays of the triangular lattice. It couples three structures: the differences within the arms must all be different (one Golomb-type condition shared by the three arms), the cross lengths a^2 + ab + b^2 are Loschian numbers that must be represented only once, and a cross length equals a within-arm length exactly when (a, b, |a' - a''|) is a triangle with a 120-degree angle, an Eisenstein triple (problem eisenstein-triples). Counting gives L(27) >= 109: the 108 or more within-arm differences are different integers below L. The exact values for small N, the growth of L(N), and how close the VLA-sized case can come to 109 are open.
references: A. R. Thompson, J. M. Moran, G. W. Swenson Jr., Interferometry and Synthesis in Radio Astronomy, 3rd ed., Springer (2017)
P. J. Napier, A. R. Thompson, R. D. Ekers, The Very Large Array: design and performance of a modern synthesis radio telescope, Proc. IEEE 71 (1983) 1295-1320
T. A. ten Brummelaar et al., First results from the CHARA Array. II. A description of the instrument, Astrophys. J. 628 (2005) 453-465 (arXiv:astro-ph/0504082)
G. S. Bloom, S. W. Golomb, Applications of numbered undirected graphs, Proc. IEEE 65 (1977) 562-570
P. Erdos, R. K. Guy, Distinct distances between lattice points, Elemente der Mathematik 25 (1970) 121-123

novelty.verdict: new question: non-redundant Y arrays are built with different baseline vectors (CHARA, MROI) and Golomb rulers solve the one-armed case; no result was found on Y arrays whose baseline lengths are all different.
closest: Non-redundant Y arrays in practice (CHARA, MROI): baseline vectors different, lengths not; on a Y that only asks for a Golomb ruler on each arm.
Golomb rulers (one arm) and distinct distances in grids (Erdos and Guy; our tri-distinct): related distinctness questions on other point sets.
Y-array design for the VLA (power-law antenna spacing for uv-coverage): a different objective.
novelty.benchmark: no array-design family in the benchmark

first_values.note: Exact values from tools/src/yarray.c (mode exact: depth-first search over arms and distances, increasing L). OEIS has no sequence with the exact terms 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 9, 11, 14, 17, 21.

baseline.text: arm length 165, held by Quantavane (Arhan Canli), 9 November 2026: the array in `refs/y-array.txt` (arms of 9, 10, 8 antennas). Lower bound 109.

bound.source: the arms carry at least 108 pairs of antennas (sizes 9, 9, 9 minimise the count), whose differences are different integers between 1 and L - 1
